terms.grammar: lūdō with sine and the ablative of rixa
terms.comment: A description of ours from two classical words: lūdere and rixa, a squabble or brawl. We have found no set phrase for telling children to play nicely in Lewis & Short, the loci collections, Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini. For playing together in general, see “play together” (collūdere); to stop a quarrel, nōlīte rixārī or nōlīte lītigāre (see “quarrel”).
With the classical adverb placidē, calmly, gently; a description of ours.

phrases.latin: reddere quī vōcēs jam scit puer et pede certō signat humum, gestit paribus conlūdere et īram colligit ac pōnit temere et mūtātur in hōrās
phrases.english: the child who can now talk and plants his feet firmly on the ground longs to play with others his age; he flares up and calms down for no reason, and changes from hour to hour

sources: Lewis & Short: rixa · Lewis & Short: rixor · Lewis & Short: placidus · Lewis & Short: ludo
